newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. finds "living skeletons" in Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.N. finds "living skeletons" in Sierra Leone.

text.p: The U.N. World Food Programme said on Friday it had found hundreds of emaciated people in Sierra Leone who looked like "living skeletons" after being held by rebels as slave labourers for up to five years.

The WFP said thousands of other people may have been been held captive. "The people we saw looked like a group of living skeletons with bundles of rags on their heads," the WFP's director in the West African state was quoted as saying.

Local WFP officials, after hearing reports that hundreds of sick and hungry people had walked long distances in a desparate search for food, said they had found a "horrific scene" at the town of Blama last Wednesday.
"Men and women were reduced to skeletons, with some of them having to support themselves on sticks to walk," the statement reported country director Mohamed Diab saying.

"Young men and women, besides being very thin, had swollen feat and sores, having walked days to reach Blama. The children had bloated stomachs, scabies and discoloured hair because of malnutrition," Diab said.

He said the people, about 500, had recently been freed by hunters organised into a civil defence force by local leaders after being held "as forced labour" by Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebels for up to five years.
But the WFP said it believed that up to 15,000 more people had also been freed by the hunters and were hiding in the dense jungle around the town of Kenema.
"One 75-year-old woman showed a scar on her head where she had been hit by a rebel for failing to work on a farm even though she collapsed from hunger," Diab said.

"Another explained how she became deaf in one ear after being hit in the ear with the butt of a rebel gun for not working. None of the captives were given any food from the harvest or looted properties," he added.
The WFP, the United Nation's food aid agency, said it was planning to send food for an intensive feeding programme for the freed people.
The agency said it fed up to half a million people in the country but the number had been steadily rising since the RUF rebels took up arms in 1991.
Last week, suspected rebels attacked a small town in northern Sierra Leone, killing 36 people, including six hospital patients.
